title: Hair loss: Who gets and causes
key_finding: AAD states hereditary hair loss (male/female pattern hair loss; androgenic alopecia) is the most common cause of hair loss worldwide and affects both men and women; women typically notice overall thinning or a widening part, men a receding hairline or bald spot on the crown. It can begin in the teens but usually starts later, and treatment works better the earlier it is started.

title: Interventions for female pattern hair loss
authors_or_org: van Zuuren EJ, Fedorowicz Z, Schoones J
key_finding: Covers 47 RCTs (5,290 women; search to July 2015). Topical minoxidil was more effective than placebo: about twice as many women had moderate-to-marked regrowth (RR 1.93, 95% CI 1.51-2.47; moderate-quality evidence), total hair count rose by about 13 hairs/cm2 (low-quality evidence), and 5% was no better than 2%. Most other interventions were tested in single studies, so no firm conclusions were possible. Hair loss came back within months of stopping treatment, and minoxidil should not be used in pregnancy or lactation.

title: The effectiveness of treatments for androgenetic alopecia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
publisher_or_journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology 2017;77(1):136-141.e5
key_finding: Meta-analysis restricted to good- or fair-quality RCTs (PubMed, Embase and Cochrane searched to December 2016). It concluded that minoxidil, finasteride and low-level laser light therapy promote hair growth in men with androgenetic alopecia, and that minoxidil is effective in women. title: Efficacy and safety of finasteride therapy for androgenetic alopecia: a systematic review
authors_or_org: Mella JM, Perret MC, Manzotti M, Catalano HN, Guyatt G
key_finding: Pooled 12 RCTs (3,927 men). Finasteride improved self-assessed hair (RR 1.81 short-term, 1.71 long-term; NNT 5.6 and 3.4) and increased hair count (long-term mean difference 24.3% vs placebo), both moderate-quality evidence. It found a moderate-quality increase in erectile dysfunction (RR 2.22, 95% CI 1.03-4.78) and a possible increase in any sexual disturbance, although discontinuation for sexual side effects was similar to placebo.

title: Acute selenium toxicity associated with a dietary supplement
key_finding: Outbreak investigation of a liquid supplement that contained about 200 times its labeled selenium content: 201 cases in 10 states, one hospitalisation. Hair loss was reported in about 72% of cases and nail discoloration or brittleness in about 61%. The authors say pharmaceutical-grade manufacturing standards could have prevented the outbreak. This was an outbreak investigation, not a controlled study.

title: Telogen Effluvium
authors_or_org: Hughes EC, Syed HA, Saleh D
key_finding: Telogen effluvium is a non-scarring, diffuse, often acute shedding of telogen hairs after physiologic or metabolic stress, hormonal change (women are more often affected, partly because of postpartum hormonal shifts) or medications. Diagnosis rests mainly on history and examination (pull test, shed-hair counts). Acute TE is generally benign, self-limited and reversible once the trigger is removed; a chronic form also exists.

title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
authors_or_org: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
key_finding: Adults should do 150-300 min/week of moderate-intensity or 75-150 min/week of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity (or an equivalent mix), plus muscle-strengthening activity. Some activity is better than none, and reducing sedentary time is recommended at all ages, though evidence was insufficient to set a sedentary threshold. Updates the 2010 WHO recommendations.

title: How Breath-Control Can Change Your Life: A Systematic Review on Psycho-Physiological Correlates of Slow Breathing
key_finding: PRISMA systematic review of slow breathing (<10 breaths/min) in healthy people; only 15 of 2,461 screened articles qualified. The evidence base was small and heterogeneous.

title: Hair loss types: Alopecia areata overview
key_finding: Alopecia areata causes hair loss, most often on the scalp or beard, usually starting as a round or oval bald patch. It is not contagious, often begins in childhood or young adulthood but can start at any age, and hair may regrow on its own (often within about a year). A sudden patch of hair loss should be seen by a dermatologist.

title: Hair loss in new moms: Dermatologist tips
key_finding: AAD explains that postpartum shedding is normal excessive shedding (telogen effluvium), caused by falling estrogen levels, and is not true hair loss. title: Hairstyles that pull can lead to hair loss
key_finding: Tight cornrows, braids, locs, buns, ponytails, updos, extensions or weaves can cause traction alopecia, as can constant rubbing from head coverings. Warning signs include pain, stinging, scalp crusts, broken hairs at the forehead and a receding hairline. Loosen styles and wear them tight only occasionally. Traction alopecia can become permanent if left untreated, so see a dermatologist early.

title: 10 hair care habits that can damage your hair
key_finding: AAD lists 10 common hair-care practices that can damage hair, with dermatologist tips. Examples: hair does not need 100 brush strokes a day (brush only to style), avoid pulling hair back tightly, space out chemical treatments, and protect hair from sun with a leave-in conditioner containing zinc oxide or a wide-brimmed hat.
